events.title: Pulcheria proclaimed Augusta
events.summary: On 4 July 414 Pulcheria, aged fifteen, was proclaimed Augusta and took over guardianship of her brother Theodosius II, displacing the prefect Anthemius. She and her sisters took public vows of virginity, turning the palace into something like a convent, and she shaped the court's piety and Marian devotion for a generation.

events.title: Augustine completes the City of God
events.summary: Begun in 413 as a reply to pagans who blamed the sack of 410 on Christianity, Augustine's De Civitate Dei was completed around 426 in 22 books. Books 1-10 refute pagan religion and its claims to have preserved Rome; books 11-22 trace the two cities, earthly and heavenly, from creation to the Last Judgement, detaching Christian hope from the fortunes of the Roman state.
scholarship: Markus, Saeculum: History and Society in the Theology of St Augustine (1970)

events.title: Orosius writes the Seven Books of History against the Pagans
events.summary: Commissioned by Augustine, the Spanish priest Orosius wrote in 416-417 a universal history from Adam to 417 designed to show that disasters had been worse before Christ. It became the most widely read history book of the Middle Ages and is an important source for the years 395-417, written with a providential optimism that Augustine himself did not share.
scholarship: Van Nuffelen, Orosius and the Rhetoric of History (2012)

events.title: 'Britain passes into the power of the Saxons'
events.summary: The Gallic Chronicle of 452 states under 441 that the British provinces, after various defeats, passed into the power of the Saxons. Gildas tells of a 'proud tyrant' (later named Vortigern) who hired Saxon mercenaries, who then rebelled; Bede dated the adventus Saxonum to 449, with Hengest and Horsa.

sources.w: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

events.debate: The Gallic chronicler's view from southern Gaul may exaggerate; archaeology shows Anglo-Saxon cemeteries from the 420s-430s in eastern England and a slow, regionally varied process. Halsall and others stress small elite migration and acculturation; genetic studies (Gretzinger et al. 2022) suggest substantial migration in the east.
scholarship: Gretzinger et al., 'The Anglo-Saxon migration and the formation of the early English gene pool', Nature 610 (2022)

events.title: The 'Groans of the Britons' to Aetius
events.summary: Gildas quotes a letter sent by the Britons to 'Agitius, thrice consul', usually identified as Aetius (consul for the third time in 446): 'The barbarians drive us to the sea; the sea drives us back to the barbarians; between these two kinds of death we are either drowned or slaughtered.' No help came.
events.debate: The identification of Agitius with Aetius rests on the 'thrice consul' title, which dates the letter to 446-454; some suggest Aegidius. Whether the barbarians were Picts and Irish or Saxons is unclear.

events.title: The Notitia Dignitatum
events.summary: The Notitia Dignitatum, a register of all civil and military offices of both halves of the empire with the units under each commander and their shield emblems, survives in Renaissance copies of a Carolingian manuscript. The eastern part reflects the situation around 395-400; the western part was updated haphazardly into the 420s.
events.detail: It lists about 180 field army units under the western magister peditum, many of them pseudocomitatenses upgraded from frontier garrisons, which Jones used to measure the western army's attrition after 395: perhaps half of the 395 field units had disappeared by c. 420 and been replaced by inferior troops. It is our main source for late Roman military organisation, fabricae (state arms factories) and civil bureaucracy, but it is a working document of uncertain completeness and some sections are stale.

sources.w: Notitia Dignitatum, pars Orientis et pars Occidentis

scholarship: Jones, The Later Roman Empire 284-602 (1964), app. II
Kulikowski, 'The Notitia Dignitatum as a historical source', Historia 49 (2000)
events.debate: Date, purpose and reliability of the western section are disputed.

events.title: Anastasius recognises Theodoric
events.summary: After years of negotiation by the senator Festus, Anastasius in 497 or 498 returned to Theodoric the palace regalia (ornamenta palatii) that Odoacer had sent to Zeno in 476, acknowledging his rule in Italy. Theodoric ruled the Romans as a Roman official in form, and the Goths as their king; the consulship and Senate continued under him.
events.debate: How far Theodoric was a Roman magistrate, a client king or a sovereign is the key question in modern accounts (Moorhead, Heather, Arnold).
scholarship: Arnold, Theoderic and the Roman Imperial Restoration (2014)

events.title: Battle of Mount Badon
events.summary: Gildas, writing in the sixth century, refers to the siege of Mount Badon (obsessio Badonici montis) as the last great British victory over the Saxons, which brought a generation of peace, in the year of his own birth. The ninth-century Historia Brittonum makes it the twelfth battle of Arthur.
events.locName: Mons Badonicus (unidentified; Bath is one candidate)

battle.significance: Gildas presents it as halting Saxon expansion for some decades, consistent with a pause in archaeological expansion in the early sixth century.

sources.w: Ecclesiastical History of the English People

events.debate: Date (c. 480-520), site and the participants are all uncertain; Arthur's association is not contemporary. Included for completeness of sub-Roman Britain.

events.title: Death of Clovis; Council of Orléans
events.summary: Clovis died in Paris on 27 November 511, months after presiding over the Council of Orléans, where 32 bishops regulated church asylum, ordination and church property in the new Frankish kingdom. His kingdom was divided among his four sons, setting the pattern of Merovingian partitions. The Pactus Legis Salicae was probably issued in his last years.

events.title: Anicia Juliana builds St Polyeuktos
events.summary: Anicia Juliana, great-granddaughter of Valentinian III and daughter of the emperor Olybrius, built the church of St Polyeuktos in Constantinople in 524-527, then the largest church in the city, with an epigram claiming it surpassed Solomon's Temple and with dimensions apparently modelled on it. Excavated in the 1960s, it is often read as an aristocratic challenge that Justinian answered with Hagia Sophia.
scholarship: Bardill, 'A new temple for Byzantium', in Bowden et al. (eds.), Social and Political Life in Late Antiquity (2006)

events.title: The Basilica Cistern
events.summary: After the Nika riots Justinian rebuilt the Stoa Basilica and beneath it constructed a vast underground cistern, 138 by 65 m, its roof carried by 336 columns, many reused, two resting on Medusa heads. It held some 80,000 cubic metres of water fed by the Valens aqueduct for the Great Palace and the Hagia Sophia quarter.

events.title: Frankish conquest of the Burgundian kingdom
events.summary: After the Burgundian king Godomar beat the Franks at Vézeronce in 524, killing Clovis's son Chlodomer, the Franks returned under Childebert and Chlothar, defeated Godomar near Autun in 532 and partitioned his kingdom in 534. The Franks now ruled almost all of Gaul; Provence followed in 537, ceded by Witiges.

sides.strength: armies of Childebert I and Chlothar I

battle.significance: Ended the last independent Burgundian kingdom and made the Franks neighbours of Ostrogothic Italy at a critical moment.

events.title: Cassiodorus publishes the Variae
events.summary: Around 537-538, as the Gothic War raged, the praetorian prefect Cassiodorus published the Variae, 468 official letters and formulae he had drafted for Theodoric and his successors, in 12 books. They are the richest picture of late Roman administration in the post-imperial West, from aqueduct maintenance to the appointment of officials. He later founded the monastery of Vivarium in Calabria, a centre of manuscript copying.
scholarship: Bjornlie, Politics and Tradition between Rome, Ravenna and Constantinople: A Study of Cassiodorus and the Variae (2013)

events.title: Khosrow takes Petra: start of the Lazic War
events.summary: The Lazi, resenting the Roman trade monopoly imposed by the general John Tzibus from the new fortress of Petra, invited Khosrow I, who marched into Lazica in 541 and took Petra, giving Persia a foothold on the Black Sea. Twenty years of war in the mountains of western Georgia followed.

sides.strength: garrison under John Tzibus, who was killed
Persian royal army with Lazic support

battle.significance: Opened the Lazic War and raised Roman fears of a Persian fleet on the Black Sea.

events.title: Visigoths complete the conquest of Spania
events.summary: Sisebut took Malaga and other Roman towns in 614-621, and around 624-625 King Suinthila captured the last Roman positions on the south-east coast. Isidore of Seville praised him as the first king to rule all of Spain. Cartagena was destroyed. The empire, at war with Persia, sent no help.
events.debate: Whether the Balearics stayed Roman (likely) and when exactly the last town fell are debated.

events.title: Heraclius abandons Syria
events.summary: After the Yarmuk, Heraclius left Antioch for Constantinople. Arab tradition has him say from a height on his way north: 'Peace be upon you, Syria, and what a fine country this is for the enemy.' He withdrew garrisons behind the Taurus and created a depopulated buffer, a zone of raids that would define the Arab-Byzantine frontier for three centuries.
events.debate: The farewell is a literary topos; Kaegi notes that Heraclius continued to direct defence from Anatolia.
scholarship: Kaegi, Byzantium and the Early Islamic Conquests (1992)
